historical_evidence.finding: Connector teammate-path quality Q_p had split-half reliability too low (Pearson r=0.215, Spearman-Brown 0.355) to treat as a stable scoutable trait; most variance is within-player half-to-half.
Structural influence residual split-half stability was confirmed: pooled-residual rho=+0.685, usage-partial rho=+0.557, indicating a reproducible player property.
Travel x fit outcome ordering survived split-half validation, with additive > irrelevant on net rating in 96% of holdout splits.
Ranked playsheet validation (counter ranking of BEST vs AVOID after defensive H2 suppression) was inconclusive due to low measurement reliability, small sample, and leakage risks.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Split-half reliability test of a half-based player trait (connector quality Q_p)
failed_approaches.why: Measurement reliability too low; the question was rated untestable (A_unanswerable) because the trait variance within-player overwhelmed between-player signal.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Validation of defensive suppression triggering effective counter plays based on H2-H1 drop
failed_approaches.why: Inconclusive results, limited by low measurement reliability, small sample, and leakage/stationarity risks.

evidence_establishes: Split-half (H1 vs H2) measurements of player-level traits can be overwhelmingly noisy, making such traits untestable for year-to-year or within-season stability without large samples.
Some split-half reliability analyses of other metrics (e.g., structural influence residuals) have successfully demonstrated stability, so not all half-based metrics are inherently untestable.
No study has directly examined whether a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether aggregating H2-H1 differentials at the team-season level across many games (82 per season) yields sufficient measurement reliability to detect a stable trait.
Whether year-to-year correlations of team-level defensive halftime adjustments are practically large enough to be detected with the available sample of ~30 team pairs per consecutive season.
The degree to which confounding by opponent quality, game script, coach/roster changes, and regression to the mean would distort estimates.
own_inferences: The direct precedent (SF-APPS-085) suggests that half-split traits can be too noisy to replicate even at modest sample sizes; if the true team-level signal is similarly weak, the question will be untestable with only 3-4 seasons of data.

Within-season split-half reliability (e.g., splitting a team's 82 games into two halves) would provide more data points (120 team-seasons) and could be used as an intermediate test, but it would measure internal consistency rather than the trait's stability across seasons and roster changes, which is typically implied by 'reliable team trait'.

Even with careful covariate adjustment (opponent offensive rating, home court, game script), the residual may retain substantial noise, and the number of independent team-season observations likely limits the power to detect a correlation smaller than ≈0.35.
uncertainties: The true magnitude of year-to-year correlation of the defensive H2-H1 effect is unknown; it could be as high as 0.5 if coaching staffs consistently excel at halftime adjustments, or near zero.

The optimal operationalization (e.g., adjusting for opponent pre-game offensive efficiency, using weighted averages, excluding garbage time) remains undefined and could substantially alter reliability.
Coaching changes, player turnover, and strategic evolution across seasons may weaken any persistent signal beyond what measurement noise already does.
The available 2025-26 season is partial, complicating cross-season analyses and possibly introducing selection effects.

historical_effect.explanation: Without the historical evidence, I might have assumed that a team-level aggregate metric over an 82-game season would be sufficiently stable to test year-to-year reliability. The retrieval of SF-APPS-085, which found a similar half-based trait untestable due to low split-half reliability, directly warns that such questions often fail because the within-variation dwarfs any between-trait signal. This shifted my assessment from a tentative 'proceed with careful power analysis' to 'do not proceed,' as the a priori likelihood of an adequately powered test appears low given the available sample and measurement noise.

blocking_constraints.text: With ~120 team-seasons spanning three full seasons and one partial, year-to-year reliability would be estimated on approximately 90 paired observations (30 teams × 3 seasonal transitions), possibly fewer after roster continuity filters. Detecting a true correlation of 0.3–0.4 would be marginally powered; a more realistic correlation of 0.2 would be severely underpowered.

Single-game H2-H1 scoring margin is highly noisy. Even after aggregation across 82 games, the team-level metric may exhibit insufficient inter-season reliability, analogous to the untestable split-half trait in SF-APPS-085.

Opponent quality, game location, score effects (e.g., garbage time), and team offensive adjustments confound the raw differential. Without a well-validated adjustment model, the trait may reflect the opposing offense's characteristics rather than the defense's halftime adjustment ability.

prior_work.summary: No earlier study directly tested whether a defense's influence on opponents' second-half vs first-half scoring change is a reliable team-level trait. The closest precedents examined split-half reliability of player-level halftime-based metrics (SF-APPS-085, untestable) and split-half stability of structural influence (SF18, supported), but none aggregated to team-season level or addressed year-to-year stability.

risks.text: Year-to-year analysis suffers from limited independent observations (~90 team-season pairs), reducing power to detect plausible correlation sizes.
Game-level H2-H1 is noisy; even after aggregating 82 games, measurement error may be substantial, as seen in SF-APPS-085.

Unadjusted differentials mix the defense's effect with opponent offensive strength, home-court advantage, and score effects; controlling for these requires a model whose residual may still retain systematic noise.
Teams with extreme first-half performance (good or bad) may regress toward the mean in the second half, producing spurious correlations if not properly accounted for.
Coaching, roster, and strategic trends shift over seasons, weakening the assumption that any halftime-adjustment trait would remain stable across years.

design.estimand: Year-to-year stability of the team-level average opponent second-half-minus-first-half scoring differential, adjusted for opponent offensive efficiency, home/away, and score differential entering the second half. The trait is defined as the random effects team intercept (or shrunken estimate) from a mixed model predicting game-level adjusted H2-H1 differential, correlated between consecutive seasons.
design.sample: NBA 2022-23 through 2024-25 regular seasons (3 full seasons, 90 team-seasons), using the completed 2025-26 regular season if available by analysis date (adding up to 30 more team-seasons). Each team-season contains all games where the team was the defense and the opponent scoring is recorded. After filtering for games with complete play-by-play and >24 minutes of non-garbage time, the expected sample is ~70–80 games per team-season.
design.power: With 90 teams-season pairs (for example, correlating 2023 measure with 2024 measure, pooled across all transitions), a two-sided test at α=0.05 can detect a true Pearson correlation of r ≥ 0.35 with ~80% power. A more realistic r = 0.20 would be underpowered (~35% power). Within-season split-half reliability (splitting games 1–41 vs 42–82) yields 120 observations and would detect r ≥ 0.25 with 80% power, but that measures internal consistency rather than seasonal stability.
design.controls: Pre-game opponent offensive rating (adjusted for rest and travel), home/away indicator, game total line as proxy for expected pace, binary indicator for games with large score differential (>15) midway through the third to proxy for garbage-time effects, and an interaction term for opponent offensive rating × halftime differential to account for whether strong offenses adjust differently.
design.falsification: 1) Null hypothesis that the previous season's measure does not predict the next season's measure after controlling for team overall defensive rating; if it does not, the trait is not independently stable. 2) Test that the defensive H2-H1 trait does not predict first-half opponent scoring in the subsequent season; a positive coefficient would indicate the measure is capturing general defensive ability rather than halftime-specific adjustment. 3) Permutation test shuffling team labels across seasons to generate an empirical null distribution of the correlation coefficient.
design.multiplicity: If multiple operationalizations (e.g., raw differential, p.p.p-adjusted, with/without garbage time) are tested, apply Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the primary family of year-to-year correlation tests, pre-registering a single primary specification.
design.decision_rule: Declare the trait reliable if the pre-registered year-to-year Pearson correlation is significantly positive (one-sided p < 0.025) AND the lower bound of a 95% bootstrap confidence interval exceeds 0.20. A Spearman correlation is reported as a robustness check but does not override the primary decision.
design.data_version: NBA stats API play-by-play, boxscore, and substitution data as of 2026-10-06, plus derived play-type possession records. Per-game files are frozen at the end of each completed season; 2025-26 regular season data is included only if the season is complete; otherwise it is used for supplementary power simulation only.
